name: Chocolate Red
lede: Chocolate Red is a dark brownish red, entry 98 in the color nomenclature that the Scottish artist Patrick Syme built from the mineralogist Werner's system, defined as a mixture of two neighboring reds.

sections.title: A name from a nomenclature
sections.body:
Chocolate Red does not come from the sweet [1]. It comes from a reference system that matched each color name to a painted swatch and to real examples from animals, plants and minerals [1][2]. Werner published a method of identifying minerals by their outward characters in 1774, and over the next forty years or so he revised a list of color terms for his students [2]. Patrick Syme, a Scottish artist, expanded that list to 108 terms in 1814 and to 110 in 1821, and added a painted swatch to each [2].

Why the word *chocolate* was chosen is undocumented in the sources we hold. What is documented is the recipe: Syme defines Chocolate Red as veinous blood red mixed with a little brownish red [1].

sections.title: Where it sits in the list
sections.body:
Syme's names are built from each other. Veinous Blood Red (number 96) is carmine red mixed with brownish black, and Brownish Purple Red (97), which he equates with a Werner term, "cherry red", is lake red darkened with brownish black and a little grey [1]. Chocolate Red is number 98, and Brownish Red (99) combines chocolate red with hyacinth red and a touch of chesnut brown [1].

The list then slides into the browns: Deep Reddish Brown is chesnut brown with a little chocolate red in it [1]. Chocolate Red is therefore the hinge where the reds darken into brown [1]. Nearby entries on the same page are [[veinous-blood-red]], [[dusty-rose-brown]], [[brownish-red]] and [[deep-reddish-brown]] [1].

sections.title: What Syme pointed at
sections.body:
For each color Syme named a real thing to hold it against [1]. For Chocolate Red the animal example is the breast feathers of the bird of paradise, and the vegetable example is the brown disk at the centre of the common marigold [1]. The illustrations in the modern edition show the same color on the breast of a bird of paradise in a 1801-06 engraving by Levaillant, on a marigold in Bulliard's flora of 1776-81, and on iron oxide in Sowerby's mineralogy of 1802-17 [1].

None of these is cacao. A reader who wants to see the color can look into the dark centre of a [[flower:marigold|marigold]] in late summer.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The screen color here, #4D3635, is a dark, slightly purplish brown; its nearest ordinary name is [[umber]], about 10 units away in ΔE [3]. It is a screen reading of a printed reproduction of a plate, so it is approximate, and the pigments of 1821 have aged since [3]. Syme filed it under the reds, but on a modern screen it reads as a brown [1][3].

Beside the plain English [[chocolate]], a much lighter and warmer brown (#7B3F00), it looks like a different color entirely [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive, 1,069 of 23,781 paintings (4.5 per cent) contain this color on at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of ΔE [4]. It is mostly a shadow color: 72 per cent of its role in a painting's lightness order is shadow [4]. The 1500s are over-represented, at 1.5 times the base rate, and the 1510s peak at 24 of 243 paintings, 2.2 times the base rate [4]. Among painters, Bronzino has it in 5 of 21 works and Pontormo in 4 of 13 [4].

In Google Books, the phrase *chocolate red* first rises above five per cent of its peak around 1812 and peaks in 1925 [5]. All archive numbers are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [4].

Chesnut brown with a little orange
Lake red mixed with black and grey
questions.answer: Veinous blood red mixed with a little brownish red

questions.q: Which flower's centre was Syme's vegetable example of Chocolate Red?
True or false: cacao was among the examples Syme used for Chocolate Red.

openers: Chocolate Red is entry 98 in Syme's 1821 color nomenclature, and the color's example in nature is the dark centre of a marigold, not cacao.
Look into the middle of a common marigold: that brown is the color a nineteenth-century artist chose to stand for Chocolate Red.
